title: Notice of Intervention and Comments of the Organization of MISO States, Inc. re the proposed tariff revisions filed by Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. under ER27-25.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )
Midcontinent Independent System                        )                         Docket No. ER27-25-000
   Operator, Inc.                                      )
                                                       )

                     NOTICE OF INTERVENTION AND COMMENTS OF
                       THE ORGANIZATION OF MISO STATES, INC.

        The Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”) submits this Notice of Intervention and

Comments regarding proposed tariff revisions filed by the Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) in the

above-captioned proceeding.1 On October 2, 2026, MISO filed proposed revisions to its Open

Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserves Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish a

Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) process including associated application and

operational requirements to enable loads greater than or equal to 200 MW and associated

generation to be studied together. MISO states the LARS Filing is intended to address the

Commission’s preliminary finding in its June 18, 2026 Show Cause Order that MISO’s Tariff may

be unjust and unreasonable because it does not provide generator interconnection study procedures

that account for the operational dynamics of serving electrically proximate Large Loads.2

        OMS cannot support LARS in its current form but recognizes the potential benefits of a

narrowly tailored process for coordinated studies of Large Loads and associated generation. OMS

has significant concerns with the proposed framework, particularly the absence of comprehensive

and enforceable protections against transmission cost shifting to existing customers, as well as


1
  Midcontinent Indep. System Operator, Inc., Large Load Addition Resource Study Process, Docket No. ER27-25-
  000 (October 2, 2026) (“LARS Filing”).
2
  Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal

                                                      1
 deficiencies in study transparency, project eligibility and readiness, coordination with existing

planning and interconnection processes, and potential impacts on competition and MISO’s

generator interconnection queue.

           Notably, OMS could support a LARS framework that facilitates reliable and efficient Large

Load integration while protecting existing customers and preserving nondiscriminatory access to

transmission, as discussed below.

    I.     NOTICE OF INTERVENTION

           OMS is a non-profit, self-governing organization comprising representatives from the

seventeen regulatory bodies with jurisdiction over entities participating in MISO and serves as the

regional state committee for the MISO region. OMS coordinates regulatory oversight among its

members, makes recommendations to MISO, the MISO Board of Directors, the Commission, and

other relevant government entities and intervenes in proceedings before the Commission to express

the positions of OMS members. OMS has an interest in this proceeding given the potential impact

to Bulk Electric System reliability, interconnection of Large Loads overseen by state and local

processes, resource adequacy, and eventual cost impacts to customers. As such, OMS files its

Notice of Intervention in this proceeding under Rule 214(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of

Practice and Procedure.3

           Service of pleadings, documents, and communications in this proceeding should be made

on the following:

           Tricia DeBleeckere                                 Brad Pope
           Executive Director                                 Legal & Regulatory Director
           Organization of MISO States, Inc.                  Organization of MISO States, Inc.
           811 E. Washington Ave., Suite 400                  811 E. Washington Ave., Suite 400
           Madison, WI 53703                                  Madison, WI 53703
           tricia@misostates.org                              brad@misostates.org

3
    18 C.F.R. § 385.214(a)(2) (2026).

                                                   2
  II.   COMMENTS

       OMS recognizes the potential benefits of coordinating studies of significant new electricity

loads and associated generation, including more efficient transmission solutions, improved

coordination, and greater certainty for customers seeking interconnection. OMS also emphasizes

the importance of integrating Large Loads reliably and efficiently while protecting existing

customers from unjust and unreasonable costs. However, the proposed LARS process raises

significant concerns regarding transmission cost allocation, ratepayer protection, study

transparency, project readiness, coordination with existing planning and interconnection processes,

and potential impacts on competition and MISO’s generator interconnection queue. In recognition

of these issues, OMS cannot support LARS in its current form but could support a filing that

addresses these concerns.

       Before implementation, MISO and the Transmission Owners must establish a just and

reasonable, enforceable framework that assigns transmission costs caused by the interconnection

and operation of Large Loads and associated generation to the responsible customers, consistent

with the Commission’s cost-causation principles. This framework must address not only directly

attributable Network Upgrades, but also subsequent transmission investments identified through

other planning processes, including associated reliability projects and Baseline Reliability Projects,

as well as potential cost shifts arising from congestion, energy prices, and ancillary service

requirements.

       Furthermore, LARS must not divert resources from MISO’s obligation to achieve its 373-

day generator interconnection queue processing commitment under its Tariff and Order No. 2023.

Given the evolving nature of Large Load integration and ongoing interconnection reforms, OMS

also recommends a five-year sunset and formal review to ensure that a separate expedited study


                                                 3
 pathway remains necessary and appropriate. OMS respectfully requests that the Commission

require these modifications and safeguards before permitting LARS to proceed.

       A. OMS Supports the Concept of Coordinated Large Load and Generation Studies,
          but Not LARS as Proposed.

       OMS supports continued consideration of a narrowly tailored process for sufficiently

mature, high-impact projects where coordinated studies provide clear benefits. Coordinated studies

of Large Loads and associated generation may identify more efficient transmission solutions,

reduce duplicative work, and improve visibility into the infrastructure needed to reliably serve new

demand. These benefits depend on credible project assumptions, coordination with other planning

processes, and appropriate cost allocation.

       That said, LARS cannot become another departure from MISO’s established generator

interconnection procedures and could create preferential treatment for certain projects relative to

those participating in the standard GIQ. OMS recognizes that the unprecedented scale and pace of

Large Load development, along with recent federal directives, may warrant consideration of a

specialized study process. Nevertheless, any such departure must be narrowly tailored, supported

by demonstrated need, and subject to appropriate safeguards to preserve nondiscriminatory access

to transmission capacity and prevent adverse impacts on existing queue participants. Consistent

with OMS's prior conditional support for the Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) process

as a limited, one-time measure, OMS believes that exceptions to established interconnection

procedures should not become permanent alternatives to the standard GIQ without a demonstrated

and continuing need.

       Accordingly, LARS cannot become a general alternative to the existing GIQ or provide

preferential access to transmission capacity without adequate safeguards for existing queue

participants and transmission customers. Expedited studies are not necessarily beneficial if

                                                 4
 unreliable assumptions, repeated restudies, cost shifting, or delays to other customers result.

OMS's willingness to consider LARS is therefore contingent upon meaningful limitations on its

scope and duration, including the five-year sunset and formal review recommended in Section G.

The Commission should evaluate LARS within MISO’s broader Large-Load integration

framework and require reliable, transparent, and cost-responsible outcomes.

        B. Transmission Cost Allocation Must Be Resolved Before Implementation.

                i.      Large Loads must bear the costs they cause.

        During the development of the LARS framework, OMS Work Groups provided feedback

that MISO’s proposal does not adequately address transmission cost allocation. The Work Groups

recommended that MISO consider Market Participant Funded Projects (“MPFPs”) for upgrades

driven by Large Loads and use MISO’s work on Transmission Cost Shifting Risk to inform the

treatment of LARS-related costs. These concerns remain fundamental. Large Loads may require

substantial transmission investments to address thermal and voltage constraints, maintain

reliability, and accommodate requested demand. Such costs should not be shifted to existing retail

customers, load-serving entities, or other transmission customers merely because upgrades are

classified as regional or reliability projects.

        OMS requests that MISO and the Transmission Owners establish a framework assigning

all costs caused by Large-Load integration to the responsible loads. This framework must address

direct and indirect network impacts, including upgrades identified through LARS subsequent

planning processes and costs arising from changes in project size, timing, configuration, or

operating characteristics. Consistent with the Commission’s cost-causation principles, costs

should reflect the burdens imposed by the customers or activities causing them. LARS should not

be implemented before this framework is resolved.


                                                  5
                ii.    Establish enforceable cost responsibility

       OMS recommends that MISO and the Transmission Owners evaluate a tariff framework

designating attributable upgrades as Market Participant Funded Upgrades (“MPFUs”), or using

another appropriate tariff-defined category that directly assigns all relevant costs to responsible

Large Loads. The framework should identify the legally obligated payer, when obligations become

enforceable, how shared upgrades are allocated, and what happens if a load or associated generator

withdraws, materially changes, or fails to enter service. Facilities service agreements or other

enforceable instruments should establish these obligations. MISO should explain how the

framework interacts with existing GIQ cost allocation and prevents Large-Load-driven costs from

being shifted to existing customers simply because upgrades are identified through regional

planning.

               iii.   Require financial assurance and protect against withdrawals

       During the development of LARS, OMS Work Groups recommended stronger financial

commitments, potentially higher upfront application fees, and financial assurance sufficient to

cover required upgrades, including consideration of obligations that survive a project’s withdrawal.

LARS should include meaningful protections against speculative applications and late withdrawals

that leave other customers responsible for costs incurred in reliance on proposed projects. MISO

should require appropriate escrow, bonds, letters of credit, or other enforceable financial

instruments before other customers face financial risk. The Tariff should specify withdrawal

consequences at each stage of the process, including after study completion, agreement execution,

and construction commencement. The responsible parties should bear attributable costs under

applicable tariffs and agreements. Cost responsibility between the load and generator should also

be expressly addressed.


                                                 6
                iv.     Prevent cost shifting across planning processes

       Network Upgrades identified through LARS may also arise in MISO Transmission

Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) studies, Expedited Project Reviews (“EPRs”), GIQ studies, or other

Large-Load studies. MISO must establish transparent rules and study processes for identifying the

projects and system needs responsible for those upgrades. An initially customer-driven upgrade

should not lose its cost attribution merely because it becomes part of a regional project or is refined

through another study. MISO should track upgrades and their underlying drivers across processes

and preserve the ability to assign and recover costs attributable to Large Loads and do so in a

manner sufficient to allow state regulators to be certain of proper cost assignment. The

Commission should require these rules to be established in the tariff and related agreements before

LARS implementation.

       C. LARS Must Remain Limited to High-Impact Loads.

       As MISO’s filing recognizes, LARS must be restricted to high-impact loads because

expedited coordinated studies could affect competition among generators and create disparate

treatment from MISO’s standard GIQ. OMS continues to support meaningful eligibility thresholds

that prevent LARS from becoming an alternative queue for a broad range of projects. MISO should

explain the basis for its proposed threshold, its relationship to other Large-Load processes and

applicable state definitions, and how eligibility will be limited to the process’s intended purpose.

       MISO should also clarify the eligibility of associated generation, including applicable

interconnection-service limits and their relationship to requested load and identified transmission

impacts. Eligibility and readiness requirements should be objective and consistently applied. OMS

does not support broadening access or lowering thresholds without demonstrating the need and

evaluating effects on study resources, queue participants, and reliability.


                                                  7
            D. MISO Must Validate the Electrical Relationship Between Load and Generation.

           Concurrent studies may be beneficial when generation and load are genuinely associated.

However, locating both within the same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”) does not necessarily

establish that generation will offset the load’s transmission impacts or produce the most efficient

network solution. OMS Work Groups previously questioned MISO’s proposed geographic scope

for LARS, its definition of electrical proximity, and the study conditions applied when the full load

is present but generation is unavailable, or when the load is offline but generation remains online.

For example, under MISO’s proposal, a generator in Montana could be paired with a large load in

Wisconsin as long as they are both located in LRZ 1, raising the likelihood of cost shifting from

increased congestion and additional networks upgrades.

           MISO should identify the assumptions supporting any credit given to associated generation,

including load size and operating characteristics, in-service dates, generation capability and

interconnection service, contractual arrangements, and transmission requirements when either

resource operates independently. Studies should evaluate credible operating conditions, including

generator outages and load-generation mismatches. MISO should also establish revalidation or

restudy triggers for material changes, delays, withdrawals, or termination of the load-generation

arrangement. Finally, MISO should explain how its LRZ-based approach satisfies applicable

Commission directives concerning electrically proximate loads and generation.4

           E. Transparency and Consideration of Alternative Transmission Technologies Are
              Essential.

           MISO should make final LARS study reports publicly available with sufficient information

to evaluate study results, alternatives, costs, and cost allocation. Each report should include:


4
    The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission recommends limiting LARS to within two substations for “electrically
    proximate” paired generation and load to mitigate cost shifting from increased congestion costs and additional
    network upgrades, consistent with the Show Cause Order at P112.

                                                         8
     1. The proposed load and generation’s size, location, timing, and material operating
       assumptions.

    2. Study models, model vintages, assumptions, and applicable planning criteria.

    3. Identified upgrades and the reliability constraints or needs they address.

    4. Alternatives considered, including non-transmission alternatives and alternative
       transmission technologies.

    5. Comparative costs, reliability impacts, implementation timelines, and material trade-offs.

    6. The rationale for the selected solution and supporting cost estimates.

    7. Each upgrade’s classification and cost-allocation methodology, including relevant
       transmission pricing zones and state locations.

    8. Interactions with other MISO planning and interconnection processes.

        OMS also recommends aligning the evaluation and documentation of Grid-Enhancing

Technologies (“GETs”) and other alternative transmission technologies with MISO’s Large Load

Application and Study Process and applicable Commission directives. Reports should explain why

alternatives are infeasible, fail to satisfy planning criteria, do not resolve identified violations, or

are less cost-effective or timely than the selected solution. These disclosures are essential to

evaluating whether upgrades are necessary, alternatives were fairly considered, and costs are

appropriately allocated. Core transparency requirements should be established in the tariff rather

than left solely to business practices manuals or discretionary reporting.

        F. LARS Must Address Restudies, Withdrawals, and Coordination Across Planning
           Processes.

        OMS Work Groups previously recommended that MISO establish a defined process for

restudies when a load, generator, or paired project withdraws after entering a study cycle. MISO

should specify restudy triggers, responsible parties, costs, timelines, and notification requirements.

These rules should address how withdrawals or material changes affect transmission solutions,

reliability assumptions, and costs assigned to other projects.


                                                   9
        MISO should also explain how LARS will coordinate with the Definitive Planning Process

(“DPP”), EPR, MTEP, and other Large-Load processes. Coordination should identify overlapping

constraints and upgrades, address differences in study models, and evaluate cumulative project

impacts. A separate study pathway must not allow incompatible projects to rely on the same

transmission capability or defer material system impacts until projects have advanced too far for

efficient resolution. MISO should demonstrate how these interactions will be managed before

initiating LARS study cycles.

       G. LARS Should Have a Five-Year Sunset and Formal Review.

       OMS Work Groups previously recommended limiting LARS to five years, followed by an

evaluation and a new Commission filing if MISO seeks to continue the process. Because LARS is

a new framework responding to evolving integration needs, its benefits and risks should be

evaluated using actual experience. A five-year sunset would allow MISO and the Commission to

assess whether LARS improves study efficiency, whether the existing interconnection queue is

being utilized as intended, and whether LARS produces reliable, cost-effective solutions without

adversely affecting other interconnection customers or shifting costs to existing ratepayers.

       The public review should address study completion times, project completion and

withdrawal rates, restudy frequency and causes, network upgrade costs, consideration of

alternative technologies, cost allocation and recovery, impacts on the standard queue, and changes

in underlying project assumptions. MISO should publish its findings and provide an opportunity

for stakeholder input before seeking an extension or proposing a successor process.

       H. LARS Must Not Interfere with Order No. 2023 Compliance.

       OMS emphasizes that developing and implementing LARS must not distract from or delay

MISO’s obligation to improve the standard GIQ process. MISO’s Order No. 2023 compliance

filings establish a 373-day interconnection-queue processing commitment. That obligation

                                                10
 remains a priority, and the need to accommodate Large Loads does not diminish the need for timely,

transparent, and nondiscriminatory generator interconnection.

        MISO should demonstrate that LARS can be administered without diverting resources

from achieving and maintaining the 373-day commitment. The Commission should require

reporting on staffing, study schedules, modeling requirements, and implementation activities, as

well as metrics measuring LARS’s effects on standard-queue delays, restudies, and resource

availability. OMS does not support expedited treatment for certain projects at the expense of other

interconnection customers. MISO must pursue efficient Large-Load integration and timely

generator interconnection together and demonstrate continued progress toward the 373-day

commitment independently of any claimed LARS benefits.

 III.   REQUEST FOR COMMISSION ACTION

For the foregoing reasons, OMS respectfully requests that the Commission:

   1. Recognize that OMS supports coordinated Large Load and generation studies in principle
      but cannot support LARS as currently proposed.

   2. Require MISO and the Transmission Owners to establish a Tariff-based cost-allocation
      framework assigning all transmission costs caused by Large Loads to the responsible loads,
      consistent with cost-causation principles.

   3. Require enforceable cost-responsibility agreements, appropriate financial assurance, and
      clear rules for withdrawals, restudies, and changes in load-generation arrangements.

   4. Require transparent study reports documenting assumptions, alternatives, GETs and other
      alternative technologies, costs, project classifications, and cost-allocation rationales.

   5. Require objective eligibility and readiness criteria, clarification of electrical proximity, and
      coordination with other planning and interconnection processes.

   6. Require MISO to propose a five-year sunset, subject to public evaluation, and a new
      Commission filing if MISO seeks to continue LARS.

   7. Require MISO to demonstrate that LARS will not impede progress toward its 373-day GIQ
      processing commitment under its Tariff and Order No. 2023.




                                                 11
 OMS appreciates the Commission’s consideration and encourages safeguards that ensure

expedited Large-Load interconnection delivers measurable benefits while preserving reliability,

protecting existing customers, and maintaining fair and timely transmission access.

 IV.   CONCLUSION

       OMS submits these Comments because a majority of OMS members support this filing.

This should not be construed to mean that all OMS members agree with all comments herein.

Individual OMS members reserve the right to file separate comments. In recognition of such, the

following members voted in support of this filing:

       Iowa Utilities Commission

       The Arkansas Public Service Commission, the Louisiana Public Service Commission, and

the Mississippi Public Service Commission voted against these comments. The New Orleans City

Council abstained from the vote on this filing. The Manitoba Public Utilities Board and the

Montana Public Service Commission did not participate in the vote on this filing.
